query: A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy has been reported in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state, with a yield strength of about 800 MPa and roughly 40% strain under lower-temperature testing, but at 1273 K it retains only 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain. For its use as an intermediate layer that transfers heat between W and CuCrZr while preserving structural integrity, what single intervention could overcome this loss of strength at elevated temperature? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the reported baseline, define the applicable thermal and mechanical boundary conditions, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Cr (~4 at%) to the TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy will stabilize a fine dispersion of a Cr-rich intermetallic (Laves) phase within the BCC matrix, thereby enhancing high-temperature yield strength retention by combining solid-solution hardening with dispersoid strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, dendritic BCC TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy exhibiting ~800 MPa yield strength and ~40% strain at lower temperatures but degenerating to 330 MPa yield strength (and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain) at 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~4 atomic percent Cr into the TiVNbTa alloy formulation.
generation.conditions: The alloy is used as an intermediate layer in a heat-transfer assembly between W and CuCrZr. Testing should occur under high-temperature conditions (approximately 1273 K) with mechanical loading up to 30–40% strain (compression/tension) to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a fine, thermally stable Laves phase precipitate that coexists with the BCC matrix along with Cr dissolution, which causes lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Cr addition promotes solid-solution hardening and triggers the nucleation of a dispersed Cr-rich Laves phase. The combined effect of increased lattice resistance to dislocation motion and the secondary phase impeding dislocation glide and crack propagation is expected to counteract the strength loss at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline performance (330 MPa yield strength at 1273 K), the Cr-doped alloy is predicted to retain a significantly higher yield strength (potentially 20–30% improvement) at 1273 K while still maintaining acceptable ductility for an intermediate layer, though the exact quantitative gain remains uncertain.
generation.baseline: Original TiVNbTa alloy with 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain at 1273 K, and ~800 MPa yield strength with ~40% strain at lower-temperature testing.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature (around 1273 K) mechanical loadings representative of intermediate layer conditions in heat transfer assemblies; tests should simulate strains up to 30–40% to ensure compatibility with operational mechanical and thermal stresses.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength enhancement at 1273 K is uncertain given that supporting evidence regarding Cr-induced phase changes comes from studies at room temperature in a chemically similar HEA system. High-temperature phase stability and mechanical performance need to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline TiVNbTa alloy and one set with ~4 at% Cr addition. Process both sets under identical conditions (e.g., vacuum arc melting with repeated re-melting for homogeneity). Characterize the microstructure (using XRD and electron microscopy) to confirm the presence of any secondary Cr-rich Laves phase. Perform mechanical tests (compression/tension tests to 30–40% strain) at 1273 K.
measurements: Yield strength and compressive strength at 1273 K
Phase identification and quantification via XRD and microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., an improvement of ~20–30% in yield strength compared to the baseline at 1273 K) or if the secondary phase formation adversely affects ductility beyond acceptable limits for an intermediate layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
